discovery: Discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and the opening of neutrino astronomy with the cubic-kilometre IceCube detector
motivation: Halzen conceived and led the realisation of IceCube, turning a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice into a neutrino telescope; Spiering pioneered deep-detector techniques (Baikal, AMANDA) and shaped the instrument and collaboration that made it possible. In 2013 IceCube discovered a diffuse flux of PeV-scale astrophysical neutrinos, a new window on the universe beyond photons and cosmic rays. Follow-up identified the blazar TXS 0506+056 (2018, in coincidence with a flare), the active galaxy NGC 1068 (2022), and neutrino emission from the Galactic plane (2023), establishing neutrino astronomy as a quantitative science. The achievement exemplifies new fundamental physics enabled by building an unprecedented observational capability and following it through with rigorous statistical care. It also tests neutrino physics at energies far beyond accelerators and links particle physics with multimessenger astrophysics.
